events.description: Husain Haqqani became Pakistan's ambassador to the United States (served to Nov 2011).
Roggio and Haqqani made a joint public appearance in early June 2021 'in the heart of the Taliban offensive', warning against the Doha agreement.
Taliban took Afghanistan by force; 'six months in' they still frame it as a victory of their ideology over the Western way of life.
Doha agreement: Khalilzad negotiated what Haqqani calls a withdrawal deal sold as a peace deal; the Taliban say their only commitment was to facilitate the US withdrawal.
After 9/11 Musharraf let US troops and flights transit Pakistan; Washington wrongly assumed Pakistan had changed its worldview.
TTP took over the tribal areas and much of the then-NWFP; the Pakistani state only moved against them when they entered Buner, 60 miles from Islamabad (year not stated by hosts).
Husain Haqqani wrote in Foreign Affairs (Aug 2021) that Pakistan sees the Taliban's return as a victory but it will be pyrrhic.
Recent Baloch militant attacks on military facilities in Balochistan.
Taliban prime minister said the Taliban did not come to power to provide bread but to impose Islam.
CENTCOM commander McKenzie stated US ISR capability in Afghanistan is 1-2% of what it was before the withdrawal.
Washington Post reported a US Army assessment of the withdrawal in which commanders said Biden officials did not understand the situation on the ground.
President Biden allocated $3.5 billion of the $7-9 billion frozen Afghan reserves for humanitarian aid ('just last week').
Khalilzad tried at the last minute to negotiate a handover of power to a committee involving Karzai; the Taliban refused.
Tehrik-e-Mujahideen raised money across India and built a base in today's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; the British destroyed the base and killed its leaders, but offshoots persisted into the 20th century.
Partition: Pakistan received 17% of British India's resources, 19% of population but 33% of its army, shaping an army in search of a threat.
Haqqani published 'Islam's Medieval Outposts' on the madrasa curriculum shortly after 9/11.

key_claims: Pakistan is the Taliban's biggest backer and lifeline (families, medical care, arms, training, money) and the ISI/military drive this policy out of an India-centric worldview.
The 'wheel of jihad': the Pakistani state supports the Afghan Taliban, the Afghan Taliban support the TTP, and the TTP attacks the Pakistani state; the Afghan Taliban will not act against the TTP.

The Taliban will never crack down on individual foreign jihadists ('brothers in faith'), so al-Qaeda and other groups are reconverging in Afghanistan even if large camps are avoided for China's or Pakistan's sake.
The Doha agreement was a withdrawal deal sold as a peace deal; the Taliban's only commitment was not to shoot departing Americans, and their emir said so publicly.
The Taliban are a Deobandi religious movement with perhaps 10-12% support that never cared about legitimacy or power sharing; Western diplomats projected their own assumptions.
Post-withdrawal 'over the horizon' CT is largely fiction: McKenzie put ISR at 1-2% of previous capability, and past successes depended on the NDS and Afghan partners.
Humanitarian aid and frozen reserves will leak to the Taliban, who already pay fighters with donated food, as Saddam's oil-for-food did.
Pakistan's 'victory' in Afghanistan is pyrrhic: a revived TTP and Baloch militancy, economic stagnation and heavy Chinese debt.
